869.title: Flame from flame
869.hook: is the one reborn the same person? like a flame lit from another flame, neither the same nor different (Milinda, Book 2)
869.carry: owing its light to the one before
869.howItsDone: Theravada teachers often explain rebirth with Nagasena's lamp images from the Questions of King Milinda: a continuing of causes, neither the same person nor a different one, with no soul passing across.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the chariot, a name for parts working together. Your line: a name for parts.

If a name is only a name for parts, the king has a sharper question waiting. Buddhists speak of rebirth. When a life ends and another begins, he asks, is the one born the same as the one who died, or someone else? It's a trap with two doors. Say the same, and there's a fixed self after all, carried from body to body. Say someone else, and why should anyone care what happens to that stranger? Nagasena takes neither door. Neither the same, he says, nor another. And then, as always, he reaches for something you could hold in your hand.
screen: `SAME PERSON, OR SOMEONE ELSE?` → `A TRAP WITH TWO DOORS.` → `NEITHER THE SAME, NOR ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: First, a lamp through the night. If a man lights a lamp and it burns all night, Nagasena asks, is the flame in the first watch the same as the flame in the middle watch? No, says the king. And the last watch? Not the same either. Then were there several lamps? No, the light burned all night from the same lamp. Just so, says Nagasena: one moment arises as another passes, and the line runs on, neither the same nor another. Second, a lamp lit from a lamp. Elsewhere in the book the king asks whether rebirth happens without anything passing over. Yes, Nagasena says. When one lamp is lit from another, no little piece of the first flame travels across. Yet the second burns, and it wouldn't without the first. Third, a verse from a teacher. The king learned verses from his teacher as a boy. Did the verse transmigrate into him? No. Yet he has it, because of the teacher. Fourth, why the image matters. A flame lit from a flame is not a soul moving house, and not a stranger either. It's a cause and what it causes, close enough to be responsible for, open enough to change. And the night-long lamp shows it within one life too: on that picture, the person who started this lesson is already a later flame of the same lamp. In the Theravada telling, what carries on is not a thing but a continuing, each flame owing its light to the one before.
screen: `ONE LAMP, BURNING ALL NIGHT.` · `A FLAME LIT, AND NOTHING PASSES OVER.` · `A VERSE LEARNED FROM A TEACHER.` · `NOT A SOUL MOVING HOUSE.` · then, large: `NEITHER THE SAME NOR ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: If you can do it safely, light one candle from another and watch the new flame catch; if not, bring the picture to mind. Then sit with the breath: each one arises from the one before, and none of them is the same breath.
Lamp. Nagasena's image for rebirth: nothing passes from one flame to the next, yet the light burns on.
Your line: owing its light to the one before. Neither the same, nor another. Day eight hundred sixty-nine.

870.title: The stolen mango
870.hook: is the thief responsible for mangoes that grew from the one he took? yes (Milinda, Book 2)
870.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use Nagasena's mango and fire cases to explain kamma and rebirth together: no fixed self passes across, yet a life is not cut off from the deeds it grew from.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the lamp, where nothing passes over, yet the new flame burns because of the old. Your line: owing its light to the one before.
screen: `OWING ITS LIGHT TO THE ONE BEFORE.`

segments.voice: Here's the loophole the king spots. If the one reborn is neither the same nor another, maybe the new one gets off clean. A fresh flame, a fresh start. Why answer for what an earlier flame did? It sounds like a legal argument, and Nagasena answers it like one. He takes the king into a courtroom. A farmer drags a man before the king: this man stole my mangoes. And the thief has a clever defense ready.
screen: `A FRESH FLAME, A FRESH START?` → `A FARMER, A THIEF, A KING.` → `A CLEVER DEFENSE.`

segments.voice: First, the defense. Your majesty, the thief says, I never took the mangoes this man planted. He put a mango in the ground; the ones I picked grew on the tree that came up from it. Different mangoes. Not guilty. Second, the verdict. Would that man deserve punishment? Nagasena asks. Yes, says the king: whatever he says, the mangoes he took grew from the one the farmer planted. Third, the turn. Just so, Nagasena says. A person does good or bad in this life, and from those deeds another name and form is born. So the deeds are not escaped. The new life grew from the old the way the fruit grew from the planted mango. He gives the king more cases of the same shape. A man lights a fire in the cold season to warm himself and walks off without putting it out. It spreads and burns a neighbor's field. The fire I lit, he says, isn't the fire that burned your field. Responsible anyway, says the king, because one fire came from the other. Fourth, what this keeps together. Yesterday's flame said nothing fixed passes across. Today's mango says that doesn't make you a stranger to your own past. Both stand at once. In this passage, kamma isn't pictured as a judge handing out sentences from outside. It's fruit growing from what was planted; no one needs to carry it from the seed. And it grows on any ordinary day, not only across lives: the word said yesterday, the promise left lying, the fire not put out.
screen: `THESE AREN'T THE MANGOES HE PLANTED.` · `GUILTY: THEY GREW FROM HIS.` · `A FIRE LEFT BURNING, A FIELD LOST.` · `KAMMA: FRUIT FROM WHAT WAS PLANTED.` · then, large: `THE MANGO GREW FROM YOURS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small thing that happened because of something you did, kind or careless: a message you sent, a door you held, or didn't. Don't argue the case or build a clever defense; just let it be yours, this grew from that, held without excuse and without punishment.
Mango. Nagasena's courtroom case: the thief is guilty, because the fruit he took grew from the one that was planted.
Your line: the mango grew from yours. Not a sentence handed down, but fruit from a seed. Until tomorrow.

871.title: Milk to curd
871.hook: milk becomes curd, then butter: continuity without a fixed thing (Milinda, Book 2)
871.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use Nagasena's milk, curd, butter and ghee image to explain how a life continues without a fixed self: each state arises from the one before.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the stolen mango, guilty because the fruit grew from what was planted. Your line: the mango grew from yours.

A baby photo, propped on a shelf. Someone tiny on their back, not yet able to hold up their own head. Is that the grown person who walks past it every morning? The quick answer is yes. But that baby had no words, none of the grown person's memories, hands a fraction of the size. So in what sense is it the same one? Nagasena puts exactly this to the king, and the king's first answer is no: that baby was someone else. Nagasena shows him what that answer would cost, and then he reaches into a kitchen.
screen: `A PHOTO OF A BABY.` → `IS THAT YOU?` → `THE KING SAYS NO.`

segments.voice: First, the cost of saying no. If the baby and the grown king are simply two different people, Nagasena says, then the king had no mother, no father, no teacher at all. The boy who goes to school would be one person and the one who finishes his learning another. The one who does a wrong would be different from the one who answers for it. The king asks what Nagasena would say instead. Second, the answer. I was that tender baby, Nagasena says, and I am this grown man, held together as one by dependence on this same body, one moment depending on the one before. Third, the kitchen. Milk is taken from the cow. After a while it turns to curd; from curd, butter; from butter, ghee. Would it be right to say the milk is the same as the curd, or the butter, or the ghee? No, says the king, but they came from it. Just so, says Nagasena: one state arises, another passes away, and the line runs on, neither the same nor another. Fourth, why a kitchen. Nobody stands over a pot of curd arguing whether it's still the milk. They know it came from the milk and wouldn't exist without it. The milk didn't hand over some hidden essence. It changed, all the way through. So the baby in the photo isn't a stranger, and isn't a frozen self either. It's milk, and the person looking at the photo is the butter.
screen: `IF THE BABY WAS SOMEONE ELSE...` · `ONE THROUGH THE SAME BODY.` · `MILK, CURD, BUTTER, GHEE.` · `NO HIDDEN ESSENCE, ONLY CHANGE.` · then, large: `IT CAME FROM THE MILK.`

segments.voice: Look for something in the middle of becoming, tea cooling, a plant leaning toward the window, light shifting across the floor, and watch it for a moment. Then let your hands rest in your lap: once they were small enough to grip one finger, and now they're changed all the way through. Nothing needs to be held still.
Curd. Nagasena's kitchen image: not the milk, and not something else either, but what came from it.
Your line: milk to butter. Changed all the way through, and still from the same milk. Day eight hundred seventy-one, done.

872.title: Why the good suffer
872.hook: the king asks why good people suffer; Nagasena answers carefully
872.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers point to this passage of the Questions of King Milinda to say that not all suffering is the result of past kamma, and that illness and accident have other causes too.

segments.voice: Yesterday: milk to curd, not the same and not another, but it came from the milk. Your line: milk to butter.

The king has heard the mango and the milk: deeds bear fruit. So he takes the idea to its edge, where it hurts. The Buddha, he says, had cleared away every unwholesome deed. Then why, in the stories, did he ever suffer? Why did a splinter of rock wound his foot? Why was he ever sick? If every pain is the fruit of something done, the king says, then either the Buddha had bad deeds left, or the teaching is wrong. Pick one. It's a question heard in hospital waiting rooms too: why did this happen to someone who didn't deserve it?
screen: `DEEDS BEAR FRUIT. SO...` → `WHY DID THE BUDDHA SUFFER?` → `PICK ONE, SAYS THE KING.`

segments.voice: First, the careful answer. Nagasena won't pick either. The mistake, he says, is in the premise: not everything that is felt has kamma as its root. Second, the list. Pain can come from several causes: from the body's own workings, what the old medicine called wind, bile and phlegm; from the change of seasons; from careless treatment; from a sudden blow from outside; and from kamma. Kamma is one cause among them, not the only one. Those who say every pain is the result of past deeds, he says, go too far. Third, the Buddha's foot. The splinter of rock was not the ripening of some old deed. It came from someone else's act and the plain fact of a stone breaking. The Buddha felt the pain. That did not mean he had earned it. Fourth, why this matters on an ordinary day. It's easy to hear the teaching on kamma as a verdict: you're sick, so you must have done something. Nagasena refuses that reading, in a book the tradition keeps. When someone is suffering, the question of what they did to deserve it may have no answer at all, because the suffering may not have come from anything they did. Bodies fail. Weather turns. Other people act. Stones fall. That leaves room for something besides judgment: room to sit beside the person, and to help. The king asked the hard question at full strength, and Nagasena answered without pretending it was easier than it was.
screen: `NOT EVERY PAIN HAS KAMMA AS ITS ROOT.` · `THE BODY, THE SEASONS, A BLOW, KAMMA.` · `THE BUDDHA'S FOOT: PAIN, NOT PAYMENT.` · `ROOM FOR HELP, NOT A VERDICT.` · then, large: `THE HARD QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that happened to someone, maybe you, that nobody deserved. You don't need to explain it or fix it; if a judgment comes, they must have, I must have, notice it and set it down. Breathe beside it, the way you might sit beside a friend.
Kamma. One cause of pain among several, Nagasena says, not the whole story, and not always the reason someone suffers.
Your line: the hard question. Some pain asks for help, not a verdict. See you tomorrow.

873.title: Like the ocean
873.hook: nibbana compared to the ocean, to a mountain peak, to space (Milinda, Book 4)
873.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often speak of nibbana by simile rather than definition, and Nagasena's comparisons to the ocean, a mountain peak and space are among those retold.

segments.voice: Yesterday: why the good suffer, kamma as one cause of pain among several, not a verdict. Your line: the hard question. Today, the goal itself.

Try describing the color blue to someone who has never seen color. Sooner or later the words turn into likenesses: cool like water, open like the sky. The king hits the same wall. He asks Nagasena about nibbana, the end of craving and suffering that the whole path points toward. Can you show me its shape, its size, its color, how long it lasts? No, says Nagasena; it can't be shown that way. Then is there nothing to say at all? There is, Nagasena answers. Its qualities can be pointed to, one simile at a time.
screen: `DESCRIBE BLUE, WITHOUT SIGHT.` → `NIBBANA: SHAPE? SIZE? COLOR?` → `NO. BUT ITS QUALITIES, BY SIMILE.`

segments.voice: First, like the ocean. The ocean, Nagasena says, is vast and boundless, and all the rivers flowing into it never fill it up. Nibbana too is not filled by all the beings who reach it. The ocean keeps no corpse; it washes it ashore. Nibbana keeps none of the corpses of the defilements: greed, hatred and delusion. Second, like a mountain peak. A peak is lofty and cannot be shaken. It's hard to climb, and seeds don't take root on the bare summit. Nibbana is high, unshakable, hard to reach, a place where the defilements can't grow, and free from liking and disliking, as a peak favors no one. Third, like space. Space is not born and does not grow old. It does not die or pass away. It can't be conquered, and thieves can't carry it off. It rests on nothing, it has no end, and birds move through it freely. Nibbana, Nagasena says, has those qualities. Fourth, why similes. Nagasena isn't hiding something; he's being honest about what words can do. A shape would make nibbana one more thing in the world, something with edges, something to grab. A simile gives a direction instead: look toward the open sea, the high summit, the clear sky, and keep looking past them. The king asked for a description and got a set of windows. Each one shows a little; none is the view itself. It's Nagasena's way of saying: this is real, and it's not an object.
screen: `OCEAN: VAST, NEVER FILLED.` · `PEAK: HIGH, UNSHAKABLE, HARD TO CLIMB.` · `SPACE: UNBORN, RESTING ON NOTHING.` · `A SET OF WINDOWS, NOT A SHAPE.` · then, large: `LIKE SPACE.`

segments.voice: Go to a window, step outside, or remember the sky from this morning, and let your eyes rest on the open part, not the clouds or buildings. Notice that it holds everything that moves through it and keeps none of it. Then let that openness be the background for the breath, with thoughts moving through like birds.
Nibbana. What Nagasena points to only by simile, the ocean, the mountain peak and space, since it can't be shown by shape.
Your line: like space. Unborn, resting on nothing, keeping nothing. That's day eight hundred seventy-three.

874.title: Kanishka's council
874.hook: the Kushan king's council in Kashmir, in the northern accounts
874.howItsDone: Northern Buddhist traditions, including Tibetan and Chinese histories, remember a council under King Kanishka, while the Theravada chronicles of Sri Lanka count their councils differently; each tradition keeps its own list.

segments.voice: Yesterday: like the ocean, nibbana pointed to by simile. Your line: like space. Today we leave the king's court and head north.

Sheets of copper, engraved line after line with commentary on the teaching, sealed inside a stupa so the words would last. That is the story the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang recorded about Kashmir. A few days ago, the Theravada chronicles of Sri Lanka remembered a council under Ashoka, and a canon written on palm leaves. Travel north, into Kashmir and beyond, and the accounts kept there remember another gathering, under another king: Kanishka, a ruler of the Kushan empire.
screen: `COPPER SHEETS, SEALED IN A STUPA.` → `THE SOUTH REMEMBERS ITS COUNCILS.` → `THE NORTH REMEMBERS KANISHKA.`

segments.voice: First, the king. In the northern accounts, Kanishka is a powerful ruler who becomes a patron of the teaching. Tradition says he was troubled because the monks he consulted gave him different explanations of the same teachings, and he wanted to know which were sound. Second, the gathering. So, the accounts say, he called learned monks together in Kashmir. Some name a monk called Vasumitra as its leader, and some link the poet Ashvaghosha with it too. Others place the meeting somewhere else. The stories agree on the king and the purpose more than on the details. Third, the work. In these accounts the monks didn't write a new canon. They wrote commentaries: long explanations of the teaching and of the finer points of the Abhidharma, the systematic analysis of mind and experience. That's where the copper sheets come in: Xuanzang recorded a tradition that these commentaries were engraved on them and sealed inside a stupa. Fourth, why it matters that the accounts differ. The Theravada chronicles of Sri Lanka don't include this council in their list. The northern schools, and the Tibetan and Chinese histories that drew on them, remember it. Nobody has to decide here which list is right. Buddhism was already more than one living tradition, with more than one memory of its own past. Each community kept the councils that shaped its own texts. Hearing the northern account doesn't cancel the southern one. It's another community, telling the story the way it was told to them.

875.title: A new wave of sutras
875.hook: new scriptures appear, centered on the bodhisattva who waits to free all beings
875.howItsDone: In Mahayana communities, sutras such as the Heart Sutra, the Diamond Sutra and the Lotus Sutra are chanted and studied, and the bodhisattva vow, to seek awakening for the sake of all beings, is taken in ceremony.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kanishka's council, remembered in the north and not in the south. Your line: the northern account. This week Nagasena lit a flame from a flame, judged a stolen mango, turned milk to curd, took on the hard question, and pointed at space.

A sutra opens the way the old ones do: thus have I heard. The Buddha is seated among his followers. But the crowd is different. Alongside the monks sit beings called bodhisattvas, whole assemblies of them, and the teaching that follows sounds new. In India, texts like this began to circulate: the Perfection of Wisdom sutras, the Lotus Sutra, and others. The communities that treasured them gave their way a name. Mahayana. The great vehicle.
screen: `THUS HAVE I HEARD.` → `A CROWD OF BODHISATTVAS.` → `MAHAYANA: THE GREAT VEHICLE.`

segments.voice: First, the figure at the center. A bodhisattva is a being set on full awakening. The word isn't new: we met the bodhisatta in the Jataka tales, the Buddha in his earlier lives, and the Theravada tradition honors that path too. What the new sutras do is hold it up as a path for many to walk, not only the one who became the Buddha. Second, the vow. In these texts the bodhisattva sets out to awaken not for themselves alone but for the sake of all beings. One popular way of putting it: the bodhisattva waits at the threshold of nibbana until every being can pass through. Some Mahayana teachers put it differently: not waiting, but working, life after life, until all are free. Either way, the heart of it is three words. For all beings. Third, a twist. The Diamond Sutra, one of the Perfection of Wisdom texts, has the Buddha say that a bodhisattva should resolve to lead all beings to nibbana, and yet hold that no being at all has been led there. If he thinks of a self, a being, a person, he is no bodhisattva. It echoes Nagasena's chariot, turned toward compassion: help everyone, and build no self out of the helping. Fourth, where the texts came from. Followers of these sutras received them as the Buddha's word. A story some tell says certain texts were kept by the nagas, serpent beings, until the right teacher came for them. Historians say simply that these texts appear later than the older collections. Both views are held.
screen: `THE BODHISATTVA: SET ON AWAKENING.` · `THE VOW: FOR THE SAKE OF ALL BEINGS.` · `HELP ALL, AND BUILD NO SELF FROM IT.` · `RECEIVED AS THE BUDDHA'S WORD.` · then, large: `FOR ALL BEINGS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who waits for others, the friend who walks at the slow one's pace, the parent who eats last, the coworker who stays until everyone's file is in, and stay with that face, noticing what their waiting gives. Then gently widen the circle, to the people around them and the people around those, as far as it will grow.
Mahayana. The great vehicle: the name taken by communities following the new sutras, with the bodhisattva and the vow for all beings at their center.
Your line: for all beings. Awakening sought not for yourself alone, but for everyone. Until tomorrow.
